about: Why each proposition is right or wrong, written from the lecture summaries Abi sends (one entry per lecture in 'lectures'). Each question entry is keyed by a short id and gives one line per option letter; the build copies it to the question's constellation stars and word-for-word copies, matching options by wording, so one entry covers every copy. If a lecture disagrees with an answer key, don't write the explanation: show Abi first (see CLAUDE.md).

groin-hernias.title: Groin hernias and other abdominal wall hernias

R54.A: That's the definition: a sudden inflammation of the bronchial lining, almost always infectious.
R54.B: The parenchyma and the alveoli are spared. Parenchymal damage means pneumonia.
R54.C: It's the most common acute lower respiratory tract infection.
R54.D: It can complicate chronic bronchitis, triggering COPD exacerbations.

R92.A: It's acute: sudden onset, and complete healing within a few weeks.
R92.B: It can complicate chronic bronchitis, triggering COPD exacerbations.
R92.C: The parenchyma and the alveoli are spared. Parenchymal damage means pneumonia.
R92.D: It's the most common acute lower respiratory tract infection.

R219.A: It's usually viral and heals on its own: no antibiotics, except in smokers with COPD or a true superinfection.
R219.B: It's the most common acute lower respiratory tract infection.
R219.C: Inflamed alveoli is pneumonia. Bronchitis inflames the bronchial mucosa and spares the alveoli.
R219.D: The parenchyma and the alveoli are spared. Parenchymal damage means pneumonia.

R86.A: Mostly viral: rhinovirus, influenza and parainfluenza, RSV, coronavirus, adenovirus.
R86.B: The diagnosis is clinical. A chest X-ray is only for a doubt about pneumonia, especially in smokers.
R86.C: No focal signs: auscultation is normal, or shows a few rhonchi or wheezes.
R86.D: No imaging is needed. A chest CT is what confirms bronchiectasis, a differential diagnosis.

R147.A: There are no focal signs. Localized signs point to pneumonia.
R147.B: Occasionally some wheezing, from post-viral bronchial hyperreactivity, especially in children.
R147.C: The diagnosis is clinical. A chest X-ray is only for a doubt about pneumonia.
R147.D: Bacteriology is generally unnecessary, even when the sputum looks purulent.
R147.E: Chest X-ray, bacteriology and virology are usually not needed.

R2.A: A hospitalization in the past year is a risk factor for dying of pneumonia.
R2.B: Fever is a symptom, not a mortality risk factor.
R2.C: Chills are a symptom of typical pneumonia, not a mortality risk factor.
R2.D: Congestive heart failure is a mortality risk factor, like chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis and COPD.

R152.A: Congestive heart failure is a mortality risk factor, like chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis and COPD.
R152.B: Fever is a symptom, not a mortality risk factor.
R152.C: A history of bacterial pneumonia is a mortality risk factor.
R152.D: Chills are a symptom of typical pneumonia, not a mortality risk factor.
R152.E: Living in an institution (nursing home, prison) is a mortality risk factor.

R212.A: Chills are a symptom of typical pneumonia, not a mortality risk factor.
R212.B: Fever is a symptom, not a mortality risk factor.
R212.C: Congestive heart failure is a mortality risk factor, like chronic kidney disease, cirrhosis and COPD.
R212.D: COPD is on the list of mortality risk factors.

R55.A: Fever is the rule: 39 to 40°C, with intense chills.
R55.B: The onset is sudden. A gradual onset suggests atypical pneumonia.
R55.C: A dense, homogeneous alveolar opacity limited to a lobe or segment, often with an air bronchogram.
R55.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading germ, 30 to 47% of cases.

R91.A: A dense, homogeneous alveolar opacity limited to a lobe or segment, often with an air bronchogram.
R91.B: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia. The leading germ is the pneumococcus.
R91.C: A sudden onset is the classic picture of typical lobar pneumonia.
R91.D: Fever is the rule: 39 to 40°C, with intense chills.

R198.A: Fever is the rule: 39 to 40°C, with intense chills.
R198.B: The onset is sudden. A gradual onset suggests atypical pneumonia.
R198.C: Herpes around the nose or mouth is a classic clue of pneumococcal pneumonia.
R198.D: A dense, homogeneous alveolar opacity limited to a lobe or segment, often with an air bronchogram.
R198.E: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia. The leading germ is the pneumococcus.

R85.B: The R in CRB-65: a respiratory rate over 30 per minute.
R85.C: Fever isn't in the score: confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age.
R85.D: The B is for low blood pressure: systolic under 90 or diastolic under 60 mmHg.

R202.A: Not a CRB-65 criterion: the score is confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age.
R202.B: 36 per minute is over 30, so it counts for the R.
R202.C: The cut-off is systolic under 90 or diastolic under 60 mmHg, not 140/80.
R202.E: Chills aren't in the score: confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age.

R227.A: The B is for low blood pressure: systolic under 90 or diastolic under 60 mmHg.
R227.D: Chills aren't in the score: confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age.

R90.A: The pneumococcus causes typical pneumonia. Atypical germs: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsiae, Legionella.
R90.B: Myalgia, mild chills and a fever under 39°C fit the atypical form.
R90.C: Leukopenia and neutropenia, the opposite of typical pneumonia.
R90.D: Nasolabial herpes is a clue to pneumococcal, typical pneumonia.

R199.A: Some crackles, but no focal signs. The X-ray shows an interstitial pattern.
R199.B: Myalgia is common in atypical pneumonia.
R199.C: Rickettsiae are atypical germs, with Mycoplasma and Chlamydia.
R199.D: The pneumococcus causes typical pneumonia. Atypical germs: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsiae, Legionella.
R199.E: Leukopenia and neutropenia, the opposite of typical pneumonia.

R234.A: Mycoplasma is the classic cause: 10 to 20% of CAP, mostly children and young adults.
R234.B: Myalgia, mild chills and a fever under 39°C fit the atypical form.
R234.C: Nasolabial herpes is a clue to pneumococcal, typical pneumonia.
R234.D: White cells are normal or low (leukopenia). A high count points to typical pneumonia.

R82.A: Lobar pneumonia is bacterial: there's no antiparasitic treatment.
R82.B: Empirical antibiotics aimed at the pneumococcus first (amoxicillin 3 g a day), started within 4 hours.
R82.C: Chest physiotherapy to clear secretions is part of the symptomatic treatment.
R82.D: Smoking cessation is the main preventive measure, with vaccination.

R87.A: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the leading atypical germ, 10 to 20% of CAP.
R87.C: The pneumococcus causes typical lobar pneumonia.
R87.D: Chlamydiae are atypical germs. Chlamydia psittaci comes from birds (pigeons, parakeets).

R83.A: Usually insidious, after a swallowing disorder.
R83.B: It sits in the basal, lower parts of the lung, where gravity takes what was inhaled.
R83.C: Abscesses are frequent, because of the anaerobes.
R83.D: Foul-smelling breath and sputum are the classic clue of anaerobes.

R1.A: Bacteria are by far the most common cause, the pneumococcus first.
R1.B: It's an alveolitis, an infection of the alveoli. An infection of the bronchi is bronchitis.
R1.C: It's the leading cause of death from infectious disease.
R1.D: Community-acquired means caught outside a hospital. Caught in hospital, it's nosocomial pneumonia.

R150.A: In the elderly it often shows as intellectual slowing rather than the classic signs.
R150.B: Behavioral changes, or a comorbidity decompensating, can be the first sign.
R150.C: It prefers the dependent, lowest parts of the lung, from chronic aspiration.
R150.D: Chronic aspiration explains the location and the germs from the mouth: anaerobes, enterobacteria.
R150.E: Radiological healing is very slow in the elderly.

R236.C: Haemophilus influenzae is one of the typical germs, after the pneumococcus.
R236.D: The pneumococcus is the leading cause, 30 to 47% of cases.

R28.A: It sits at the base of the right lung.
R28.B: There's usually a history of intestinal or liver amoebiasis.
R28.C: Entamoeba histolytica is a parasite: it responds to anti-amoebic treatment (metronidazole), not antivirals.
R28.D: Its vomica is brown, chocolate-coloured. A hydatid vomica comes from a hydatid cyst.

R81.A: It sits at the base of the right lung, not the left.
R81.B: Its vomica is brown, chocolate-coloured. A hydatid vomica comes from a hydatid cyst.
R81.C: Metronidazole treats it, and improving on anti-amoebic treatment confirms the diagnosis.
R81.D: There's usually a history of intestinal or liver amoebiasis.

R201.A: A brown, chocolate-coloured vomica is the classic clue of an amoebic abscess.
R201.B: There's usually a history of intestinal or liver amoebiasis.
R201.C: Metronidazole treats it, and improving on anti-amoebic treatment confirms the diagnosis.
R201.D: It sits at the base of the right lung, not the apex.
R201.E: Foul-smelling breath points to anaerobic bacteria, not the amoeba.

R80.A: Once it drains, the X-ray shows a round cavity with thick walls and an air-fluid level.
R80.B: The early stage starts insidiously over 2 to 3 weeks: fever, chills, chest pain, purulent sputum.
R80.C: It's mostly bacterial (pyogenic): streptococci, staphylococci, Gram-negative bacilli, anaerobes.
R80.D: Pus in the pleura is a pleurisy (empyema). An abscess is pus in a new cavity inside the lung.

R200.A: Pus in a cavity that already existed (bulla, cyst, cystic bronchiectasis) is excluded: the cavity must be new.
R200.B: Tuberculosis is excluded: the cause must be an acute, non-tuberculous infection.
R200.C: It's a medical emergency that needs fast, effective treatment.
R200.D: When it bursts into a bronchus, the patient coughs up a large amount of pus: the vomica.
R200.E: After the vomica, the cavity shows an air-fluid (hydroaeric) level.

R78.B: They come especially in winter, often as outbreaks.
R78.C: The X-ray shows an interstitial syndrome: fine reticular or micronodular opacities, on one or both sides.
R78.D: They can: influenza and COVID-19 caused pandemics.

R148.A: They're usually mild, and the outcome is generally good.
R148.B: They come especially in winter, often as outbreaks.
R148.C: The X-ray shows a diffuse interstitial syndrome, not a localized opacity.
R148.D: They spread as seasonal outbreaks, even pandemics.
R148.E: Bronchial hyperreactivity is one of the long-term airway after-effects.

R89.A: Severe edema in the interstitium can leave fibrosis later.
R89.B: Influenza starts suddenly: chills, fever, headache, body aches.
R89.C: Bacterial superinfection is common (H. influenzae, pneumococcus, staphylococcus).
R89.D: Without a superinfection, the fever falls in two phases: the influenza V.

R149.A: It's a zoonosis: a coronavirus of animal origin (bats) that crossed over to humans.
R149.B: SARS-CoV-2 is the coronavirus behind COVID-19.
R149.C: It spreads through the air, by droplets and aerosols, hence masks.
R149.D: Hands carry it too, which is why hand washing is part of prevention.

R58.A: Most of the germs are endogenous: from the patient's own sinuses, mouth, stomach and esophagus.
R58.B: It counts up to 7 days after discharge, not a month.
R58.C: Hand washing is the most emphasized preventive measure.
R58.D: Death occurs in 30 to 50% of cases.

R197.A: Signs must appear at least 48 hours after admission. Earlier, it was already incubating.
R197.B: Gram-negative bacilli lead: enterobacteria, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella.
R197.C: It still counts up to 7 days after discharge.
R197.D: Ventilator-associated pneumonia starts after 48 hours of ventilation, not 12.
R197.E: Its incidence is highest in intensive care units.

R79.A: Delayed or poorly matched antibiotics worsen the prognosis.
R79.B: Age over 60 is the poor prognostic factor, not youth.
R79.C: Comorbidities are a poor prognostic factor.
R79.D: The bad germs are MRSA, Pseudomonas, fungi or several germs at once, not streptococci.

R151.A: Age over 60 is the poor prognostic factor, not youth.
R151.B: MRSA is one of the germs that worsen the prognosis, with Pseudomonas and fungi.
R151.D: Spread on the X-ray is a poor prognostic factor.
R151.E: Delayed or poorly matched antibiotics worsen the prognosis.

R88.A: The risk factor is losing the cough reflex, which leaves the airway unprotected.
R88.B: Anemia with hemoglobin under 10 g/dl is a risk factor.
R88.D: The risk factor is age over 70.

R21.A: Most of the germs are endogenous: from the patient's own sinuses, mouth, stomach and esophagus.
R21.B: It's very frequent in ventilated ICU patients: ventilator-associated pneumonia.
R21.C: The delay is at least 48 hours after admission.

R124.A: It can be found by chance on a scan done for something else.
R124.B: The patient often looks generally well.
R124.C: The X-ray can be normal. With bronchorrhea or hemoptysis, that should still raise suspicion.
R124.D: HRCT confirms it. Bronchoscopy looks for a local cause (foreign body, tumor, compression).
R124.E: Medical treatment is given in every case. Surgery comes after it, for localized forms.

R174.A: It's acquired in most cases, after infection and inflammation damage the bronchial wall. Congenital causes are rare.
R174.B: Abnormal systemic-type vessels grow in the bronchial wall and bleed easily.
R174.C: Bronchorrhea, a heavy purulent sputum, is the main symptom.
R174.D: Clubbing is uncommon overall. It's very common only in the diffuse form.
R174.E: HRCT confirms it. Bronchoscopy looks for a local cause (foreign body, tumor, compression).

R246.A: Clubbing can be present, very commonly in the diffuse form.
R246.B: HRCT is the confirmatory test (tram tracks, signet ring sign).
R246.C: The dilation is irreversible: that's the key word of the definition.
R246.D: It's a dilation of the bronchi (sub-segmental, over 2 mm), not a disease of the alveoli.

R29.A: Surgery is only for localized forms, after medical treatment has failed.
R29.B: Bronchodilators help clear the airway but don't treat an infectious flare-up.
R29.C: Inhaled corticosteroids aren't the treatment of a flare-up.
R29.D: A flare-up needs antibiotics, with airway clearance (chest physiotherapy) to drain the sputum.

R65.A: Airway clearance (chest physiotherapy, hydration) is central: it breaks the infection and mucus cycle.
R65.B: Treatment is medical first. Surgery is for localized forms after medical treatment, with good lung function.
R65.C: True: the FDA approved brensocatib in August 2025, the first drug for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis. It's not in the lecture.
R65.D: The dilation is irreversible: that's the key word of the definition.

R30.A: Protect the airway, then image the chest to find where it bleeds before embolization or surgery.
R30.B: Abundant hemoptysis can be fatal: it needs active management.
R30.C: Steroids don't stop bleeding. The steps are hemostatic treatment, then embolization, then surgery.
R30.D: Anticoagulation would make the bleeding worse.

R40.A: A reduced FEV1 fits COPD just as well.
R40.B: Daily copious purulent sputum (bronchorrhea) is the hallmark of bronchiectasis.
R40.D: Smoking points to COPD, not bronchiectasis.

R109.A: The dilation is irreversible: that's the key word of the definition.
R109.B: It's chronic and irreversible, not an acute reversible inflammation.
R109.C: Infection and mucus stasis feed each other, so flare-ups keep coming back.
R109.D: It's either localized or diffuse, and diffuse forms affect the lungs unevenly.

R161.A: For recurrent hemoptysis, surgical excision is the most definitive treatment.
R161.B: Infections that keep coming back in a localized form, despite treatment, can justify removing it.
R161.C: Surgery needs good lung function: impaired function argues against it.
R161.D: A lung abscess is a complication that can call for removing the diseased area.
R161.E: Surgery comes after well-conducted medical treatment has failed.

R240.A: Pus around the lung (purulent pleurisy) is an infectious complication.
R240.B: Diffuse forms can lead to amyloidosis.
R240.C: Sarcoidosis is a separate disease, not a complication.
R240.D: A lung abscess is an infectious complication.

R271.A: They come especially in winter, often as outbreaks, not in summer.
R271.C: Vaccination against influenza and COVID-19 helps prevent them, with hand washing and masks.
R271.D: The X-ray shows an interstitial syndrome: fine reticular or micronodular opacities, on one or both sides.

R272.A: Not a CRB-65 criterion: the score is confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age.
R272.D: Oxygen saturation isn't in the score: confusion, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age.

R273.A: It can suction secretions, but a superinfection is treated with antibiotics.
R273.B: It looks for a local cause: a foreign body, a tumor, a compression.
R273.C: HRCT confirms the diagnosis, not bronchoscopy.
R273.D: It shows the state of the bronchial mucosa and where the secretions or bleeding come from.

R274.A: Influenza is the most common of the viruses that infect the lungs.
R274.B: It's highly contagious: it spreads as epidemics, even pandemics.
R274.C: Group A mutates a lot, which is why it causes most epidemics and the pandemics.
R274.D: The incubation is short: 2 to 4 days.

R275.A: It can be found by chance on a scan done for something else.
R275.B: The X-ray can be normal. With bronchorrhea or hemoptysis, that should still raise suspicion.
R275.C: The patient often looks generally well.
R275.D: Medical treatment is given in every case. Surgery comes after it, for localized forms.

R277.A: Legionella is an atypical germ. The leading germ of lobar pneumonia is the pneumococcus.
R277.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading germ, 30 to 47% of cases.
R277.C: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia. The leading germ is the pneumococcus.
R277.D: Chlamydia psittaci is an atypical germ, caught from birds.

R278.A: Myalgia is common in atypical pneumonia.
R278.B: The pneumococcus causes typical pneumonia. Atypical germs: Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsiae, Legionella.
R278.C: It often starts like a cold, with catarrh of the upper airways.
R278.D: Some crackles, but no focal signs. The X-ray shows an interstitial pattern.

R279.A: The exam finds a condensation syndrome: increased vocal fremitus, dullness, crackles.
R279.B: The onset is sudden. A gradual onset suggests atypical pneumonia.
R279.C: Fever is the rule: 39 to 40°C, with intense chills.
R279.D: A dense, homogeneous alveolar opacity limited to a lobe or segment, often with an air bronchogram.

R280.A: Community-acquired means caught outside a hospital. Caught in hospital, it's nosocomial pneumonia.
R280.B: It's the leading cause of death from infectious disease.
R280.C: It's an alveolitis, an infection of the alveoli. An infection of the bronchi is bronchitis.
R280.D: Bacteria are by far the most common cause, the pneumococcus first.

R281.A: Patient education is part of it: the outlook, the long-term treatment, daily airway clearance.
R281.B: Surgery is only for localized forms, not diffuse ones.
R281.C: Antibiotics are for superinfections, not given all the time.
R281.D: Clearing ENT and dental infections is part of the management.

R282.A: It counts up to 7 days after discharge, not 15.
R282.B: Signs must appear at least 48 hours after admission. Earlier, it was already incubating.
R282.C: Gram-negative bacilli lead: enterobacteria, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella.
R282.D: Its incidence is highest in intensive care units.

R283.A: Delayed or poorly matched antibiotics worsen the prognosis.
R283.B: Age over 60 is the poor prognostic factor, not youth.
R283.C: Comorbidities are a poor prognostic factor.
R283.D: The bad germs are MRSA, Pseudomonas, fungi or several germs at once, not streptococci.

R284.A: It can complicate chronic bronchitis, triggering COPD exacerbations.
R284.B: Inflamed alveoli is pneumonia. Bronchitis inflames the bronchial mucosa and spares the alveoli.
R284.C: It goes through two phases: a dry cough first, then a productive one.
R284.D: It's usually benign and heals completely within a few weeks.

R285.A: It lives in hot water systems and air conditioning, and spreads through their droplets.
R285.B: Extra-respiratory signs are marked, digestive and neurological.
R285.C: Beta-lactams don't work on it: macrolides or fluoroquinolones.

D38.A: Obstruction of the lumen is the main cause. Stasis lets germs multiply, then the wall turns ischemic.
D38.B: Lymphoid hyperplasia of the wall is one cause, along with fecaliths, worms or foreign bodies.
D38.C: The lumen opens into the cecum, which is how the colon's septic contents reach it.
D38.D: The muscle layer's peristalsis empties the lumen. Lymphoid tissue also destroys germs.

D146.A: The muscle layer's peristalsis empties the lumen. Lymphoid tissue also destroys germs.
D146.B: The lumen opens into the cecum, which is how the colon's septic contents reach it.
D146.C: Hematogenous spread is a cause, though exceptional. Obstruction is by far the main one.
D146.D: Clinical examination can rarely tell complicated from uncomplicated forms: the classic anatomoclinical dissociation.

D203.A: The muscle layer's peristalsis empties the lumen. Lymphoid tissue also destroys germs.
D203.B: Obstruction of the lumen is the main cause. Stasis lets germs multiply, then the wall turns ischemic.
D203.C: The lumen opens into the cecum, which is how the colon's septic contents reach it.
D203.D: Clinical examination can rarely tell complicated from uncomplicated forms: the classic anatomoclinical dissociation.

D37.A: Pain on dropping onto the heels has the best predictive value for peritoneal irritation.
D37.B: The general condition is usually preserved.
D37.C: Fever is moderate, 37.8 to 38.5°C; a higher fever suggests a complication.
D37.D: Tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point, the outer third of the umbilicus to iliac spine line, is the key sign.

D156.A: Rectal and vaginal exams are part of the workup: normal at first, sometimes painful on the right.
D156.B: Murphy's sign belongs to acute cholecystitis, not appendicitis.
D156.C: Fever is moderate, 37.8 to 38.5°C; a higher fever suggests a complication.
D156.D: Pain on dropping onto the heels has the best predictive value for peritoneal irritation.

D50.A: Prothrombin time doesn't help the diagnosis. At most it's part of the pre-anesthetic workup.
D50.B: The blood count shows leukocytosis over 10,000/mm³, mostly neutrophils.
D50.C: CRP is raised. With the blood count, it backs up the clinical diagnosis.

D169.A: Right iliac fossa pain with moderate fever is the typical picture.
D169.B: A subhepatic appendix, from incomplete rotation, gives pain in the right upper quadrant.
D169.C: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder is biliary, as in cholecystitis.
D169.D: Left iliac fossa pain with fever suggests sigmoid diverticulitis.

D68.A: The base sits 2 cm below the end of the terminal ileum.
D68.B: The base lies where the three taeniae coli meet, so following them leads to it.
D68.C: Haustra don't help locate the appendix.
D68.D: Only the base is constant. The tip can point in many directions.

D71.A: Antibiotics and analgesics only support surgery, which treats the cause.
D71.B: It can be done by laparoscopy or by laparotomy.
D71.C: The removed appendix is always sent for pathology, which can find a tumor such as a carcinoid.
D71.D: It's a surgical emergency: appendectomy, by laparoscopy or laparotomy.

D152.A: A collected abscess can be drained percutaneously under ultrasound or CT guidance.
D152.B: Patients are hospitalized in a surgical unit.
D152.C: Antibiotics go with drainage. Alone, they don't treat a collected abscess.
D152.D: An abscess needs draining and antibiotics, not just removal of the appendix.

D205.A: Pregnant women tend to present late, which makes the diagnosis harder.
D205.B: A pelvic appendix gives rectal tenderness, and obesity dulls all the local signs.
D205.C: A retrocecal appendix is often silent: little rigidity, sometimes no tenderness even on deep pressure.

D31.A: Diarrhea isn't on the list. Constipation is, because straining raises abdominal pressure.
D31.B: Dysuria makes the patient strain, which raises abdominal pressure.
D31.C: Asthma and its coughing raise abdominal pressure.
D31.D: Hypertension doesn't raise abdominal pressure. The factors are asthma, dysuria and constipation.

D153.A: Asthma and its coughing raise abdominal pressure.
D153.B: Straining at stool raises abdominal pressure.
D153.C: Dysuria makes the patient strain, which raises abdominal pressure.
D153.D: Diarrhea isn't on the list. Constipation is, because straining raises abdominal pressure.

D35.A: It swells and tenses on coughing. Losing that impulse is a sign of strangulation.
D35.B: There is no spontaneous pain and none on palpation.
D35.C: It can be pushed back into the abdomen, and the swelling disappears.
D35.D: Signs of obstruction point to strangulation, a surgical emergency.

D198.A: It can be pushed back into the abdomen, and the swelling disappears.
D198.B: It swells and tenses when the patient coughs: the cough impulse.
D198.C: An uncomplicated hernia is painless. Pain suggests strangulation.
D198.D: Signs of obstruction point to strangulation, a surgical emergency.

D36.A: That defines an incisional hernia. In evisceration the wall and skin are open, after a wound gives way.
D36.B: That's the definition: protrusion through a natural weak point of the abdominal wall.
D36.C: That's the definition: protrusion through a weakness left by previous surgery, under intact skin.
D36.D: Diastasis recti is a gap of more than 2 cm between the rectus muscles.

D190.A: Diastasis recti is a gap of more than 2 cm between the rectus muscles.
D190.B: That's the definition: protrusion through a weakness left by previous surgery, under intact skin.
D190.C: That's the definition: protrusion through a natural weak point of the abdominal wall.
D190.D: That defines a hernia. In evisceration the wall and skin are open, after a laparotomy gives way or a penetrating wound.

D48.A: Its sac follows the inguinal canal and can reach the scrotum: an inguinoscrotal hernia.
D48.B: Like any hernia, it can strangulate.
D48.C: It's congenital, from a persistent peritoneovaginal canal. The acquired weakness hernia is the direct one.
D48.D: It's seen in newborns and young adults. Adults and the elderly get direct hernias.

D155.A: Like any hernia, it can strangulate.
D155.B: It can reach the scrotum. The direct hernia is the one that never does.
D155.C: It's seen in newborns and young adults. Adults and the elderly get direct hernias.
D155.D: It's congenital, from a persistent peritoneovaginal canal. The acquired weakness hernia is the direct one.

D148.A: Hernias are very common, a frequent reason for consultation.
D148.B: They don't heal on their own and can strangulate. Surgery is the only definitive treatment.
D148.C: They occur at any age, newborns included.
D148.D: That's the definition: protrusion through a congenital or acquired defect of the wall.

D27.A: No neutralizing: milk or any other oral antidote is on the list of mistakes to avoid.
D27.B: Rinsing the mouth with saline is one of the right first steps, not a mistake.
D27.C: Never induce vomiting: the caustic would burn the esophagus a second time on the way up.
D27.D: No lying flat: the patient is kept half seated.

D75.A: Intubate if there's respiratory distress or severe consciousness disturbances, and only then.
D75.B: Correcting hypovolemia and acid-base imbalances is part of the first steps.
D75.C: Keep the upper airway open, give oxygen, and IV corticosteroids if the larynx is swollen.
D75.D: No nasogastric tube: it's on the list of mistakes to avoid.

D157.A: No neutralizing with milk or any other antidote: it's a mistake to avoid.
D157.B: No gastric lavage: it's on the list of mistakes to avoid.
D157.C: The patient is kept half seated, never lying flat.
D157.D: Never induce vomiting: the caustic would burn the esophagus again on the way up.

D200.A: Half seated is the right position. It's lying flat that's avoided.
D200.B: No left jugular or subclavian line: the left neck may be needed for an emergency cervical approach.
D200.C: Rinsing the mouth with saline is one of the right first steps.
D200.D: Neutralizing with milk or another oral antidote is a mistake to avoid.

D39.A: The esophagus and stomach are the main targets. Lesions beyond the pylorus are less common.
D39.B: Management is multidisciplinary: anesthesiologist, emergency physician, surgeon, radiologist, ENT, psychiatrist.
D39.C: Severity depends on the product's nature, pH, concentration, form and the amount swallowed.
D39.D: Suicide attempts are the most common cause: 9 out of 10 ingestions are voluntary.

D141.A: In children, ingestion is usually accidental.
D141.B: The esophagus and stomach are the main targets, not the jejunum or colon.
D141.C: Suicide attempts are the most common cause: 9 out of 10 ingestions are voluntary.
D141.D: It's a medical and surgical emergency with significant mortality.

D40.A: Labels should stay on and labeling rules be followed.
D40.B: Special safety caps are part of primary prevention.
D40.C: Caustics must never go into food or drink containers, where they get mistaken for a drink.
D40.D: Siphoning caustic products is a classic accident, so it's to be avoided.

D67.A: Labels should stay on and labeling rules be followed.
D67.B: Keeping household products out of children's reach prevents accidental ingestions.
D67.C: The opposite: never put caustics into food containers, where they get mistaken for a drink.
D67.D: Prevention campaigns on TV and in the media are part of primary prevention.

D29.A: Edema and hyperemia of the mucosa is grade 1. Grade 2A is superficial, non-circumferential ulceration.
D29.B: Grade 1 is only edema and hyperemia. Small areas of necrosis are grade 3A.
D29.C: Grade 3B is extensive necrosis. 3A is limited necrosis.
D29.D: Grade 2B means circumferential ulcerations. In 2A they don't go all the way round.

D151.A: Past surgical history isn't a severity factor. The product and how much was swallowed are.
D151.B: The product's nature, acid, base or oxidant, is the first severity factor.
D151.C: A very low (under 2) or very high (over 12) pH means more severe lesions.
D151.D: Diabetes isn't a severity factor. Severity comes from the product, its pH, concentration and amount.

D193.A: Oxidants like bleach are the most common caustics, but a pH under 2 or over 12 does the most damage.
D193.B: Strong acids like hydrochloric acid cause coagulation necrosis.
D193.C: Bases cause liquefaction necrosis, which hits the esophagus more than the stomach.
D193.D: Coagulation necrosis spreads little in depth: it leaves superficial eschars, not diffuse wall damage.

D26.A: Headache and neck pain aren't warning signs of esophageal cancer.
D26.B: Progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids, is the leading symptom (74% of patients).
D26.C: Odynophagia, pain on swallowing, is one of the warning symptoms.
D26.D: Weight loss is the second most common symptom, in 57% of patients.

D139.A: Odynophagia, pain on swallowing, is one of the warning symptoms.
D139.B: Weight loss or loss of appetite is common, in 57% of patients.
D139.C: Neck pain isn't a warning symptom. Hoarseness or cervical lymph nodes are.
D139.D: Headache isn't one of the symptoms to look out for.

D49.A: Reflux leads to Barrett's esophagus and adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.
D49.B: Tobacco is a major risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma.
D49.C: Alcohol is a major risk factor, especially together with tobacco.
D49.D: Nitrosamines, made from nitrites and nitrates in food, are a dietary risk factor.

D64.A: Reflux, through Barrett's esophagus, is the main risk factor for adenocarcinoma.
D64.B: Tobacco and alcohol are risk factors for both types, above all squamous cell carcinoma.
D64.C: Menopause isn't a risk factor. Esophageal cancer is mostly a disease of men.
D64.D: Diet matters: nitrosamines, barbecue, canned foods and very hot drinks raise the risk.

D43.A: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type.
D43.B: Epidermoid carcinoma is another name for squamous cell carcinoma, not a second type.
D43.C: Adenocarcinoma is the other main type, arising on Barrett's esophagus.
D43.D: Sarcomas are rare: each uncommon type makes up under 1% of esophageal cancers.

D70.A: Staging the disease, local, regional and distant, comes before any treatment plan.
D70.B: A clinical assessment comes first, of both the patient and the disease.
D70.C: The plan is decided in a multidisciplinary panel discussion.
D70.D: A head CT is only done for warning signs, not routinely.

D195.A: The chest and abdominal CT is for staging, once the diagnosis is made.
D195.B: Abdominal MRI plays no part in diagnosing esophageal cancer.
D195.C: A barium swallow is only used when the endoscope can't get past a complete stenosis.
D195.D: Upper endoscopy with biopsies confirms the diagnosis and locates the tumor.

D32.A: Humans are accidental hosts, a dead end for the parasite's cycle.
D32.B: In over 70% of cases, the liver is the only organ involved.
D32.D: Dogs are the definitive hosts. Sheep and other ungulates are the transient hosts.

D149.A: The liver comes first. The lungs are the second most common location.
D149.B: Humans are accidental hosts. The cycle runs between dogs and sheep.
D149.C: It's non-immunizing, so reinfestation is possible.
D149.D: Dogs are the definitive hosts. Sheep and other ungulates are the transient hosts.

D34.A: Type 4 is the pseudotumoral form: heterogeneous, with anechoic and echogenic areas.
D34.B: Type 1 is univesicular: a round, anechoic, pure liquid cyst. Multivesicular is type 3.
D34.C: Type 2 is the detached, doubled membrane.
D34.D: Type 5 is the calcified cyst. Pseudotumoral is type 4.

D201.A: Type 3 is multivesicular: a honeycomb of daughter cysts.
D201.B: Type 5 is the calcified cyst. Pseudotumoral is type 4.
D201.C: Type 1 is univesicular, pure liquid. Multivesicular is type 3.
D201.D: Type 2 shows membrane doubling: the membrane has come away from the wall.

D207.A: Type 3 is multivesicular: a honeycomb of daughter cysts.
D207.B: Type 1 is univesicular, pure liquid. Multivesicular is type 3.
D207.C: Type 2 is membrane doubling. Univesicular is type 1.
D207.D: Type 4 is the pseudotumoral form: heterogeneous, with anechoic and echogenic areas.

D33.A: The simple form is often asymptomatic, found by chance on an ultrasound or CT.
D33.B: Compression of the bile ducts and rupture into them, with cyst material migrating, both cause jaundice.
D33.C: Most are found at the simple stage: by chance, or from pain and a mass as it grows.
D33.D: Infection is the most common complication and can reveal the cyst.

D138.A: Contact with dogs is a frequent finding in the history, not a constant one.
D138.B: Rupture into the bile ducts also causes jaundice, as cyst material migrates into them.
D138.C: The simple form is often asymptomatic, found by chance on an ultrasound or CT.
D138.D: Most are found at the simple stage: by chance, or from pain and a mass as it grows.

D47.A: Home slaughter lets dogs eat infected offal, which closes the cycle.
D47.B: Poor hygiene raises the risk of swallowing eggs shed in dog feces.
D47.C: Sharing food spaces with infected dogs exposes you to the eggs in their feces.
D47.D: Deworming by a vet is prevention. Doing it yourself at home is what raises the risk.

D65.A: Fewer stray dogs means fewer definitive hosts spreading eggs.
D65.B: Deworming dogs with anthelmintics is one of the pillars of control programs.
D65.C: That's a risk factor, not a control measure.
D65.D: Home slaughter is a risk factor. Control programs enforce strict slaughter standards.

D136.A: Reducing the stray dog population is one of the pillars of control programs.
D136.B: Deworming or handling infected dogs at home raises the risk. Dogs should be registered and dewormed properly.
D136.C: Home slaughter is a risk factor. Control means veterinary checks and no clandestine slaughtering.
D136.D: Sharing food spaces with infected dogs is a risk factor, not a control measure.

D66.A: CL is the undifferentiated cystic lesion stage the WHO added to Gharbi's classification.
D66.B: CE4 and CE5 are the inactive, late stages.
D66.C: CE1 and CE2 are the active stages.
D66.D: CE3 is transitional, between the active and inactive stages.

D145.A: Only types 2 and 3 swap places: CE5 and Gharbi type 5 are both the calcified cyst.
D145.B: CE3 is transitional. Only CE1 and CE2 are active.
D145.C: CL is the undifferentiated cystic lesion stage the WHO added to Gharbi's classification.
D145.D: CE1 and CE2 are active. CE3 is the transitional stage.

D46.A: Perdromo's directed transparieto-hepatic fistulization is one of the conservative fistula treatments.
D46.B: A simple suture can close the fistula, typically when it's small.
D46.C: Repair over a Kehr drain in the bile duct is another option.
D46.D: A cysto-biliary fistula is a contraindication to PAIR.

D142.A: Serology (ELISA, immunoelectrophoresis) confirms the diagnosis in 80 to 95% of cases and is used for follow-up.
D142.B: The brain is a rare location. A cerebral CT is only for neurological signs.
D142.C: Ultrasound is the basis of diagnosis: it finds 90% and shows the location, content and number of cysts.
D142.D: Bone is a rare location. The routine search for other cysts is a chest X-ray, for the lungs.

D160.A: Here it means antiparasitic drugs: albendazole, for inoperable patients or multiple or disseminated cysts.
D160.B: Radiotherapy has no place in treating a hydatid cyst.
D160.C: Puncture, aspiration, scolicide injection, re-aspiration, guided by ultrasound or CT. Not with a cysto-biliary fistula.
D160.D: Surgery is the gold standard treatment.

D185.A: Bone is a rare location of hydatid disease, not somewhere a liver cyst ruptures into.
D185.B: Rupture into the thorax gives a pleural effusion with lower chest pain and dyspnea.
D185.C: Rupture into the bronchi gives a hydatid vomica. Bile in the sputum means a bilio-cysto-bronchial fistula.
D185.D: Rupture into the peritoneum, spontaneous or after trauma, can cause peritonitis or anaphylactic shock.

D186.A: Eggs survive on the ground for weeks to months: 1 month at 20°C, 15 months at 7°C.
D186.B: The adult has three parts: the head (scolex), the neck and the body.
D186.C: The germinal layer, held by a laminated membrane, buds small vesicles that make protoscolices.
D186.D: The eggs form in the last segment of the body, the gravid proglottid, not the head.

D196.A: Three forms: the adult worm, the egg and the metacestode, which is the hydatid cyst.
D196.B: Eggs survive on the ground for weeks to months: 1 month at 20°C, 15 months at 7°C.
D196.C: The eggs form in the last segment of the body, the gravid proglottid, not the head.
D196.D: The adult lives as a saprophyte between the villi of the dog's small intestine.

D44.A: The transverse mesocolon splits the cavity into two levels: supra-mesocolic and sub-mesocolic.
D44.B: That's the definition: a serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity.
D44.C: It has two parts: parietal, lining the walls, and visceral, around the organs.
D44.D: It's a closed sac in males. Only in females is it open, at the ends of the fallopian tubes.

D137.A: It has two parts: parietal, lining the walls, and visceral, around the organs.
D137.B: In disease it perceives pain, mounts the inflammatory and immune response and has fibrinolytic activity.
D137.C: Two levels, not three: supra-mesocolic and sub-mesocolic.
D137.D: In health its fluid lubricates the viscera, allowing easy movement and peristalsis.

D210.A: Its fluid, under 100 ml, lubricates the viscera for easy movement and peristalsis.
D210.B: Closed in males. In females it opens at the ends of the fallopian tubes.
D210.C: It has two parts: parietal and visceral.
D210.D: The deck doesn't tie the germ to the level: peritonitis can be chemical, bacterial, or chemical then bacterial.

D28.A: Three types: primary, secondary (the most frequent) and tertiary.
D28.B: Primary peritonitis is often monomicrobial: pneumococcus, streptococcus, Koch's bacillus, staphylococcus.
D28.C: It can stay localized, like a plastron, or spread to the whole cavity.
D28.D: Secondary peritonitis is the most common. Tertiary is an infection that persists after adequate treatment.

D204.A: It can stay localized, like a plastron, or spread to the whole cavity.
D204.B: Secondary peritonitis is the most frequent, mostly from a GI perforation or a nearby septic site.
D204.C: Primary, secondary and tertiary, with secondary by far the most common.
D204.D: With no intra-abdominal source, it's usually one germ: pneumococcus, streptococcus, Koch's bacillus, staphylococcus.

D41.A: At first the general condition is preserved. It deteriorates later, with toxic-infectious shock.
D41.B: The patient is anxious from the start.
D41.C: Fever comes early, 39 to 40°C when the peritonitis is bacterial. It can come later if chemical.
D41.D: The face is tense, from pain, dehydration and infection.

D154.A: Fever is often early: 39 to 40°C in bacterial peritonitis, later in chemical peritonitis.
D154.B: A tense face, from pain, dehydration and infection, is one of the first general signs.
D154.C: They're clear from the start: anxiety, tense face, fast pulse, high fever. Shock follows if untreated.
D154.D: At first the general condition is usually preserved, before toxic-infectious shock sets in.

D73.A: Midline laparotomy or laparoscopy both work. Laparoscopy is avoided in shock.
D73.B: Medical treatment goes alongside surgery: fluids, antibiotics, nasogastric suction, analgesics.
D73.C: Peritoneal fluid is sampled first thing on opening, to adjust the antibiotics.
D73.D: Surgery is the mainstay, done fast, to treat the source and wash out the cavity.

D74.A: Fibrinolytic activity is one of its roles in disease.
D74.B: It mounts an inflammatory and immune response, with fluid rich in immunoglobulins and phagocytes.
D74.C: Irritation of its nerve endings gives the pain and the abdominal contracture.
D74.D: In disease it feels pain, fights infection and has fibrinolytic activity.

D143.A: Wound infection is an early complication: infected tissues heal poorly, with wall abscesses and dehiscence.
D143.B: Untreated, it leads to septic shock, multi-organ failure and death.
D143.C: An incisional hernia after the laparotomy is a classic late complication, like adhesive bowel obstruction.
D143.D: Prognosis also depends on the patient's age and on how quickly they're operated on.

D158.A: Not one of the paths of infection: it's parasitic seeding from a ruptured hydatid cyst.
D158.B: Germs can reach the peritoneum through the blood, during a septicemia.
D158.C: Exogenous contamination: drains, open surgery, trauma, peritoneal dialysis.
D158.D: Ascites alone isn't a route in. Infected ascites in cirrhosis comes from germs crossing the bowel wall.

D165.A: Infection can spread from the female genital tract, as in salpingitis.
D165.B: Not one of the paths of infection: it's parasitic seeding from a ruptured hydatid cyst.
D165.C: The blood route: a septicemia can seed the peritoneum.
D165.D: GI perforation is the main route: perforated ulcer, appendix or diverticulum.

D191.A: The CT is for doubtful cases, suspected sigmoid diverticulitis, or ruling out pancreatitis.
D191.B: The diagnosis is clinical. The X-ray may show pneumoperitoneum, but a normal one doesn't rule it out.
D191.C: Procalcitonin tells infection apart from plain inflammation.
D191.D: Blood tests assess severity: blood count, CRP, electrolytes, kidney and liver tests, blood gas.

D192.A: Not one of its functional signs. Tenesmus shows up only in pelvic localized forms.
D192.B: Pain is the main sign: sudden, very intense, stabbing and rapidly generalized.
D192.C: Vomiting blood points to GI bleeding. Peritonitis gives food, then bilious, then fecaloid vomiting.
D192.D: Transit stops, usually constipation from reflex ileus, sometimes diarrhea.

D208.A: Sudden, intense, stabbing pain that quickly spreads is the leading sign.
D208.B: Nausea and vomiting are among the functional signs.
D208.C: Not a sign of peritonitis. Only pelvic forms bring urinary symptoms, and then it's dysuria.
D208.D: Vomiting blood suggests GI bleeding, not peritonitis.

D209.A: The CT is for doubtful cases, suspected sigmoid diverticulitis, or ruling out pancreatitis.
D209.B: The X-ray can show pneumoperitoneum, but the diagnosis is above all clinical.
D209.C: White cells rise above 10,000/mm³, mostly neutrophils.
D209.D: Procalcitonin tells infection apart from plain inflammation.

D30.A: Unexplained weight loss is one of the warning symptoms to ask about.
D30.B: Persistent vomiting is a warning sign, often from an obstructed gastric outlet.
D30.C: Predominant epigastric pain and early satiety are both warning symptoms.
D30.D: Lower limb edema isn't one of the warning symptoms of gastric cancer.

D92.A: Unexplained weight loss is a warning symptom. With abdominal pain, it's the classic pair.
D92.B: It's the opposite: loss of appetite and early satiety are what to look for.
D92.C: Lower limb edema isn't one of the warning symptoms of gastric cancer.
D92.D: Migraine has nothing to do with gastric cancer.

D99.A: Petechiae aren't a sign of it. Its skin signs are acanthosis nigricans and Leser-Trelat.
D99.B: Lower limb edema isn't one of the warning symptoms of gastric cancer.
D99.C: Appetite drops, with early satiety. It doesn't increase.
D99.D: Signs of GI bleeding are warning symptoms: hematemesis, melena, iron deficiency anemia.

D103.A: Lower limb edema isn't one of the warning symptoms of gastric cancer.
D103.B: It's the reverse: unexplained weight loss is one of the warning symptoms.
D103.C: Predominant epigastric pain and early satiety are both warning symptoms.
D103.D: Migraine has nothing to do with gastric cancer.

D42.A: H. pylori is the main modifiable risk factor, especially for the intestinal type.
D42.B: Family history of gastric cancer is a non-modifiable risk factor.
D42.C: It's a diet low in fresh vegetables that raises the risk, not a high-fiber one.
D42.D: A diet high in salt and nitrites is a classic risk factor.

D106.A: Fruit and vegetables protect. The risk is a diet low in fresh vegetables.
D106.B: Occupational exposure isn't on the list of modifiable risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, alcohol, obesity, salt, radiation.
D106.C: A past cholecystectomy isn't a risk factor for gastric cancer.
D106.D: H. pylori infection is the leading modifiable risk factor.

D107.A: Occupational exposure isn't on the list of modifiable risk factors: H. pylori, smoking, alcohol, obesity, salt, radiation.
D107.B: Smoking and alcohol are both modifiable risk factors.
D107.C: A past cholecystectomy isn't a risk factor for gastric cancer.
D107.D: Fruit and vegetables protect. The risk is a diet low in fresh vegetables.

D166.A: Occupational exposure isn't on the list of modifiable risk factors. Radiation exposure is.
D166.B: Radiation exposure is one of the modifiable risk factors.
D166.C: Smoking and alcohol are both modifiable risk factors.
D166.D: H. pylori infection is the leading modifiable risk factor.

D69.A: Subtotal gastrectomy with lymph node dissection treats distal, antral intestinal-type tumors.
D69.B: A feeding jejunostomy only feeds the patient. It leaves the tumor in place.
D69.C: It isn't one of the curative operations, which are total and subtotal gastrectomy.
D69.D: Total gastrectomy with lymph node dissection treats proximal and body tumors, and the diffuse type.

D91.A: It isn't one of the curative operations, which are total and subtotal gastrectomy.
D91.B: Total gastrectomy with lymph node dissection treats proximal and body tumors, and the diffuse type.
D91.C: Colectomy isn't an operation for gastric cancer. The curative ones are total and subtotal gastrectomy.
D91.D: A feeding jejunostomy only feeds the patient. It leaves the tumor in place.

D109.A: It isn't one of the curative operations, which are total and subtotal gastrectomy.
D109.B: Subtotal gastrectomy with lymph node dissection treats distal, antral intestinal-type tumors.
D109.C: A feeding jejunostomy only feeds the patient. It leaves the tumor in place.
D109.D: Bypass surgery is palliative, for an obstructed gastric outlet. It leaves the tumor in place.

D72.A: The supplement needed is B12, not folate, because intrinsic factor is lost with the stomach.
D72.B: Splitting meals is a must after gastrectomy, with no fast sugars if there's dumping syndrome.
D72.C: Vaccines are only for a splenectomy (flu, pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus), not the whole program.
D72.D: No stomach means no intrinsic factor: B12 by IM injection every 6 months, or macrocytic anemia follows.

D93.A: A bone density scan isn't part of the mandatory follow-up.
D93.B: PET isn't mandatory. Follow-up is history, exam, and CT when indicated.
D93.C: Splitting meals is a must after gastrectomy, with no fast sugars if there's dumping syndrome.
D93.D: The vitamin to replace is B12, not the fat-soluble ones.

D108.A: No stomach means no intrinsic factor: B12 by IM injection every 6 months, or macrocytic anemia follows.
D108.B: B12 must be supplemented after a total gastrectomy, or macrocytic anemia follows.
D108.C: Vaccines are only for a splenectomy (flu, pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus), not the whole program.
D108.D: The supplement needed is B12, not folate, because intrinsic factor is lost with the stomach.

D45.A: Peritoneal washing with cytology is done during the staging laparoscopy.
D45.B: It's a staging tool, not a treatment. It doesn't relieve symptoms.
D45.C: It finds peritoneal spread that imaging misses, which can change or rule out surgery.
D45.D: Its main use is looking for peritoneal carcinomatosis, in T3/T4 or diffuse-type tumors.

D102.A: Its main use is looking for peritoneal carcinomatosis, in T3/T4 or diffuse-type tumors.
D102.B: It finds peritoneal spread that imaging misses, which can change or rule out surgery.
D102.C: It doesn't spread the tumor. It looks for spread that's already there.
D102.D: It's a staging tool, not a treatment. It doesn't relieve symptoms.

D94.A: An ENT exam isn't a required step. The plan rests on staging the disease.
D94.B: Vitamin levels aren't needed. Nutrition is judged by weight, BMI and nutrition scores.
D94.C: Tuberculosis screening isn't part of the gastric cancer workup.
D94.D: Treatment depends on the stage: local, regional and distant extension (TNM), plus the patient's fitness.

D95.A: MRI can't confirm it. Only biopsies taken at endoscopy can.
D95.B: CT is for staging once the diagnosis is made, not for confirming it.
D95.C: Upper endoscopy with biopsies is the diagnostic test of choice.
D95.D: A barium swallow can't take biopsies, so it can't confirm the diagnosis.

D96.A: Diagnosis is hard: biopsies are often negative, since the tumor spreads under the mucosa.
D96.B: Linitis infiltrates the whole stomach wall, so only a total gastrectomy can remove it.
D96.D: Past surgery isn't one of its risk factors. The diffuse type is linked to hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.

D97.A: Linitis has a bad prognosis: an infiltrating signet ring cell cancer, often found late.
D97.B: A partial gastrectomy can't clear a cancer infiltrating the whole wall. It needs a total gastrectomy.
D97.D: Diagnosis is hard: biopsies are often negative, since the tumor spreads under the mucosa.

D98.A: Lymph node spread is common, so resection always includes a lymph node dissection.
D98.B: Combining surgery with chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy gives the best results. Perioperative FLOT is the preferred plan.
D98.C: Caught early, it can be cured by resection. Most patients just present late.
D98.D: Linitis is a malignant infiltrating cancer with signet ring cells, not a benign metaplasia.

D100.A: A head CT isn't routine. Staging relies on CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.
D100.B: Supportive care can start, but the treatment plan needs staging first.
D100.C: Treatment depends on the stage: local, regional and distant extension (TNM), plus the patient's fitness.
D100.D: A lipid panel plays no part in staging gastric cancer.

D101.A: Distant spread is assessed by CT, not by endoscopy.
D101.B: Confirming the diagnosis is one of its roles, so one statement is correct.
D101.C: It does locate the tumor, as well as seeing it and taking biopsies.
D101.D: Endoscopy with biopsies confirms the diagnosis. It's the test of choice.

D104.A: A head MRI isn't part of the gastric cancer workup.
D104.B: Colonoscopy isn't part of the gastric cancer workup.
D104.C: Every plan, curative or palliative, is decided in a multidisciplinary discussion.
D104.D: A CBC is part of the workup, but it doesn't decide the treatment. The panel does.

D105.A: It does locate the tumor, as well as seeing it and taking biopsies.
D105.B: Endoscopy takes biopsies, at least 10 for a good-quality diagnosis.
D105.C: Distant spread is assessed by CT, not by endoscopy.
D105.D: It's the first-line test for any suspected gastric cancer.

D110.A: Surgery is the main treatment. Chemotherapy is given around it, or alone when palliative.
D110.B: Linitis is a malignant infiltrating cancer with signet ring cells, not a benign metaplasia.
D110.C: It has a place: after surgery for large or node-positive tumors, and in palliative care.
D110.D: Nodes are involved early, so resection includes a lymph node dissection (at least 15 nodes).
